01.note: Rabbi Ahai asked two scholars, Rabbi Dostai bar Rabbi Yannai and Rabbi Yosei bar Keifar, to bring back his silver vessel from Neharde'a. The people holding it handed it over, then asked the two to perform an act of acquisition making them responsible for it on the way. When they refused, the people demanded the vessel back. Rabbi Dostai agreed; Rabbi Yosei refused, so the people tormented him, and Rabbi Dostai told them, "Hit him." Back home Rabbi Yosei complained, and Rabbi Dostai explained that these frightening men would restrain or kill on command; once Rabbi Ahai learned they were close to the government and had servants at their bidding, he told Rabbi Dostai he had acted well.
01.why: The Gemara is asking who bears responsibility for property sent through an agent and when the sender may take it back. Just before, Rav Sheshet's agent dodged a similar acquisition; this case adds holders who demand the item back, and an agent excused because he faced danger.

people.name: Rabbi Ahai, son of Rabbi Yoshiya
people.about: Owner of a silver vessel kept in Neharde'a, who sent the two scholars to bring it to him.

people.name: Rabbi Dostai bar Rabbi Yannai
people.about: One of the two agents; he agreed to return the vessel and told the holders to hit his companion.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei bar Keifar
people.about: The other agent; he refused to give the vessel back and was tormented for it.

terms.meaning: A formal legal act that transfers ownership or responsibility. Here, performing one would have made the agents answerable for the vessel until it reached its owner.
A city in Babylonia where the vessel was being kept.

02.note: Two disciples, Rabbi Yonatan ben Asmai and Rabbi Yehuda, son of converts, took leave of their teacher Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai in the evening and came back to take leave again in the morning, explaining that he had taught them a disciple who stays the night in the same city must do so twice. Impressed, Rabbi Shimon sent his son to them for a blessing. The son found them working through contradictions between verses; when they noticed him, they wished on him that he sow and not reap, bring in and not take out, that his house be destroyed, and that he not see a new year. He came home hurt, but his father told him these were all blessings in disguise, and began decoding them: he would have sons and they would not die, bring in brides for them, and his daughters' husbands would not die.
02.why: The Gemara has been reading the verses about Solomon dedicating the Temple and sending the people home; the disciples draw their practice of a second farewell from those very verses.

people.name: Rabbi Yonatan ben Asmai
people.about: A disciple of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai who, with his study partner, gave the puzzling blessing.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda, son of converts
people.about: Rabbi Yonatan's study partner, also a disciple of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai
people.about: The teacher of the two disciples; he sends his son to them and then explains their words.

terms.meaning: A formal farewell a student gives his teacher before departing. The disciples hold that if a student stays overnight in the city afterward, he must take leave again.
A commandment or religious duty from the Torah.

02.flag: The story stops partway through Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai's explanation: the decoding of the last three blessings (house and lodging, the table, the new year) falls in the segments after it.

03.note: A dying man left one son a barrel of earth, another a barrel of bones, and a third a barrel of wool wads; Rabbi Bena'a worked out that he meant land, livestock and quilts. In another case, a man overheard his wife admit that only one of her ten sons was his, so on his deathbed he left everything to "one son." Rabbi Bena'a told the sons to go strike their father's grave until he rose to tell them; the one who refused was the true son and got the property. The others slandered Rabbi Bena'a to the king, who imprisoned him, until his wife posed the guards a riddle only he could solve. Freed and made a judge at the gate, he corrected two inscriptions there, and the authorities added his versions as the sayings of the Jewish elders.
03.why: The Gemara has just mentioned Rabbi Bena'a, who examined burial caves and gazed at Adam's heels, and now gathers further incidents showing his wisdom.

people.name: Rabbi Bena'a
people.about: A Sage who solves riddles in wills, is jailed after slander, and is freed and made a judge for his wisdom.

people.name: the wife of Rabbi Bena'a
people.about: She frees her husband by posing a riddle about a 'servant' that only he can explain.

terms.meaning: A container for drinking water made from an animal's hide. The wife's 'servant' was a goat that was slaughtered, eaten, and its skin made into one.
City gates were where judges sat to hear cases; seating him there meant appointing him a judge.

03.flag: Joins two separate Rabbi Bena'a incidents: the barrel riddle and the case of the one true son.
